How a feature ships

I take features from the problem to a reviewed pull request myself, so engineering starts from working software instead of a mockup.

  1. Discovery and PRDCustomer interviews, the problem in one page, the metric that says it worked.
  2. Prototype in ClaudeA clickable version with real data shapes, ready to put in front of users.
  3. Branch and buildCodex on a branch off main, iterating against staging.
  4. Pull requestA preview link anyone on the team can open and test.
  5. Review and releaseEngineers review, harden and ship to production.

Where payment workflows break

A payment looks like one button. Behind it are five stages, and each one fails in its own way. This is what I design for.

  1. CaptureInvoices arrive by email, WhatsApp and paper, and about 1 in 7 needs a person to fix it.Extraction that shows what it isn't sure of, field by field.
  2. ComplyDeadlines carry penalties: 15 or 45 days for small suppliers in India, 30 days to register an e-invoice.Due dates computed from supplier status, with the queue sorted by consequence.
  3. ApproveInvoices take 9.2 days on average, mostly waiting for someone to look.Approval wherever the approver already is: Slack, email or phone.
  4. PayInstant rails settle in seconds, so a wrong payee can't be caught afterwards.Payee checks on the approval screen, before the money moves.
  5. ReconcileSent isn't done. Failed and returned payments disappear if nobody tracks them.Every state visible, and the result written back to the ERP.

Notes on payments, October 2026

Where payment workflows break, and how I design for them

Most payment products look simple at the Pay button. The hard work is everything around it: invoices that don't match, approvals that stall, payees nobody verified and payments that never reconcile. These are the patterns I rely on, from building payables and connected banking at Pazy.

Instant rails removed the undo window

India's UPI handled 24.07 billion payments in September 2026, about 802 million a day.1 In the euro area, banks have had to send instant credit transfers since 9 October 2025, at the same price as a standard transfer.2

When money lands in seconds, nobody gets a quiet hour to notice a wrong account number. Every check a finance team relies on has to happen before the send button. That one fact moves most of the design work upstream, into capture, approval and payee checks.

Design the exception path first

In Ardent Partners' 2025 benchmarks, 14% of invoices are exceptions and 53% of AP professionals name exceptions as their biggest problem. Only 32.6% of invoices go through without a human touch, against 49.2% for the best teams. Processing an invoice costs $9.40 on average and $2.78 at best-in-class.4

So the happy path is not where an AP team spends its day. At Pazy, AI capture read invoices at 95% accuracy, but CFOs only started using it once every extracted field showed its confidence and could be overridden in one click. CFO activation went from 12% to 68% in eight weeks. The lesson I took: show people exactly what the system isn't sure about, and make fixing it cheaper than ignoring it.

Deadlines belong in the data model

In India, Section 43B(h) gives buyers 15 days to pay a registered micro or small supplier, or 45 days under a written agreement. Pay later and the expense can't be deducted until the year it is actually paid.5 Since 1 April 2025, businesses with turnover of ₹10 crore or more must register e-invoices within 30 days, or the portal rejects them.6

A payables product that treats a due date as a field someone types in will miss both. The better pattern computes the deadline from the supplier's status and the contract, then sorts the queue by what a delay would cost, so the riskiest invoice is always at the top.

Approvals stall where people aren't

The average invoice takes 9.2 days to process.4 Most of that is waiting for an approver who is in meetings, on the road or simply not logged in to the finance tool.

At Pazy we stopped asking approvers to come to us. They approve from Slack, email or the mobile app, with routing by amount, vendor and cost centre and every action written to an audit trail. Completion went from 67% to 94% over four iterations, each one driven by where people dropped off.

Check the payee before approval

Since 9 October 2025, euro-area banks must offer a free Verification of Payee check on every credit transfer, instant or not. The payer sees one of four results: match, close match, no match or other. Banks outside the euro area have until 9 July 2027. Business customers can opt out, which matters for bulk runs, and a payer who proceeds after a warning carries the risk.23

The stakes are visible in the UK, where banks reimbursed 88% of money lost to authorised push payment scams, £173 million, in the first year of mandatory reimbursement to September 2025.7 The EU's PSD3 and PSR deal of 27 November 2025 goes further, with payee checks for all transfers and full refunds for bank impersonation fraud once the rules apply.8

For product design this means the name check belongs on the approval screen, next to the amount. In a bulk run each line needs its own state, and a close match should be a decision with the evidence beside it. Try it below: the run stays locked until every flagged payee is confirmed or removed.

A payment isn't finished until it reconciles

On 22 November 2025 Swift ended the coexistence of old MT messages and ISO 20022 for cross-border payments, so banks now exchange richer, structured payment data.9 That data only helps if the product carries it through to the books.

The status model is where this shows. Draft, awaiting approval, scheduled, sent, failed, returned and reconciled should each be visible, and failures should come back into someone's queue on their own. At Pazy, connected banking across 14+ Indian banks reported payment status in real time, and sync with Tally, Zoho Books and Oracle put a status marker on every record. Clients closed their books 10x faster.

EstateMin, June 2026 to now

Letting probate attorneys sign off on AI-drafted court documents

EstateMin's AI drafts probate documents from estate data, but the attorney is legally responsible for whatever gets filed. I designed the layer between the two, and I own the roadmap, pricing and revenue target behind it.

Role
Head of Product and Design
Team
Five people, pre Series A
Customers
50+ US probate firms
Scope
Product, design, pricing

The problem

Probate is document-heavy and deadline-driven. An AI that drafts petitions and inventories saves firms hours, but only if attorneys can check its work quickly. If checking takes as long as writing, they stop using it.

The core insight was that attorneys don't review data. They review documents. A table of extracted fields asks them to rebuild the petition in their heads before they can judge it.

What made it hard

Liability sits with the attorney

Nothing can reach a court without a person signing off, so the design had to make sign-off fast without making it careless.

Trust varies by passage

A county name pulled from a death certificate is safe. A statement about who is qualified to serve as executor needs a closer look. One confidence score for the whole document would hide that.

A team of five

Every design decision had to be buildable by a small engineering team in weeks.

What I did

  1. Made the document the interface. Attorneys review the actual petition, with AI-written passages highlighted inline by confidence level.
  2. Showed the source for every passage. A side panel shows exactly which estate record each sentence came from, so checking a claim takes one click.
  3. Borrowed maker-checker from banking. The AI is the maker and the attorney is the checker. The approve button stays locked until every conflict is resolved, and every decision is logged for compliance.
  4. Owned pricing and packaging. New firms now sign at more than twice the earlier price, and more of them activate in their first weeks.
  5. Prototyped in code. I build working prototypes in Claude, iterate on staging through Codex and open pull requests for engineering review, so we test decisions on working software.

Results so far

2x+price point for newly signed firms
25%+rise in new-firm activation
50+US probate firms on the platform
5people on the team when I joined

Firms also report getting value from the product sooner after onboarding.

What I learned

Regulated industries already have good answers to the trust problem. Maker-checker has protected bank payments for decades, and attorneys understood it immediately.

A locked button turned out to be a feature. It gave attorneys confidence that the system wouldn't let them make a mistake under deadline pressure.

Pazy.io, February 2025 to January 2026

Getting CFOs to trust AI with their invoices

Pazy builds payments and accounts-payable software for Indian finance teams. I joined as Head of Product and Design when it had a few pilot clients and no design system, and helped take it to 150+ enterprises and ₹3,000 Cr+ in invoices processed.

Role
Head of Product and Design
Team
2 designers, 8 engineers, 1 PM
Stage
Seed, ₹6 Cr raised
Platforms
Web, Android, iOS

The problem

Indian finance teams run vendor payments, reimbursements, tax reconciliation and procurement across separate tools, spreadsheets and paper. Payments arrive late, tax credits get missed and nobody can see spend in real time.

Pazy had raised ₹6 Cr in pre-seed funding from Inuka Capital and Gemba Capital to fix this. When I joined, the product had early traction but no coherent vision, design system or information architecture. My job was to build all three while shipping to live customers.

What made it hard

Enterprise complexity, consumer expectations

Invoices, purchase orders, multi-level approvals, tax checks, bank integrations and audit trails all had to feel as simple as a consumer payments app.

Three very different users

CFOs want control and dashboards. Accountants want speed. Approvers want to say yes from their phone. One product had to serve all of them.

Finance teams don't experiment

They have to trust the platform before they move money through it. Early on, only 12% of CFOs activated. The AI's output had to be easy to check before they would rely on it.

What I did

  1. Interviewed 15+ finance teams across BFSI, retail and manufacturing to map how payments actually move, from invoice capture to reconciliation.
  2. Organised the product by transaction lifecycle. Capture, approve, pay and reconcile, which is how finance teams think, replaced a menu of features.
  3. Made AI review collaborative. Every field the AI extracted shows a confidence state, and finance leaders can override it in one click. This took CFO activation from 12% to 68% in eight weeks.
  4. Took approvals to where approvers already were. Approvers can act from Slack, email or the mobile app, with routing by amount, vendor or cost centre. Completion went from 67% to 94% over four iterations.
  5. Built the design system before the screens. 180+ components and 400+ tokens mapped to code, so engineering could grow from 3 to 8 developers without the product drifting.
  6. Ran a simple prioritisation model with the founder: every feature scored on pain, frequency and revenue impact, shipped in two-week cycles and checked in Mixpanel.

Inside the product

AI invoice capture reads bills from email, WhatsApp, Slack and paper at 95% accuracy and cuts manual entry by 80%. Connected banking pays vendors across 14+ Indian banks without leaving Pazy. ERP sync keeps Tally, Zoho Books and Oracle up to date, with a status marker on every record.

What I learned

Finance teams value reliability over delight. Every state and transition had to say that the money is safe.

The design system felt slow for the first month and paid for itself every month after. When a second designer joined, they were productive within days.

The approval flow only worked once it met people in Slack, email and on their phones. A portal-only version would have failed however well it was designed.

CoinDCX / Okto, 2023 to 2024

Making DeFi usable for 20 million people

CoinDCX, India's largest crypto exchange, built Okto as a self-custody super wallet. I led product design while Okto grew from 1M to 20M users, with founders and PMs setting the direction alongside me.

Role
Lead Product Designer
Team
4 designers, 12 engineers, 2 PMs
Growth
1M to 20M users
Platforms
iOS, Android

The problem

By 2023 users wanted self-custody, access to many chains and real yield, more than a trading account on an exchange. Okto was CoinDCX's answer. But it had been built for crypto-native power users, and the next 19 million were new to DeFi.

What made it hard

DeFi is technical by nature

Gas fees, chain selection, slippage and bridge times all had to fade into the background for new users, without taking controls away from traders.

People think in assets

Users don't care which chain a token lives on. A single portfolio across EVM, Solana, Aptos and Hyperliquid needed patterns the industry didn't have yet.

Speed against safety

Futures at up to 50x leverage need instant feedback, but money movements need deliberate confirmation.

What I did

  1. Designed around five user journeys: discover, buy, trade, earn and withdraw. Every new feature had to fit one of them.
  2. Hid advanced settings one tap away. Slippage, gas and routing stay out of the way until someone wants them. Try the pattern below.
    You pay120 USDTPolygon
    You get0.031 ETHBase

    Network fee paid in USDT. No ETH needed.

    Advanced settings
    Slippage
    0.5%
    Route
    Polygon to Base, 1 bridge
    Fee token
    USDT

  3. Made cross-chain swap a single tap, with gas paid in any token the user already holds. That removed the biggest drop-off in DeFi onboarding. The swap flow went through six iterations, shaped by weekly sessions with traders and casual users.
  4. Brought futures to a six-inch screen with panels traders can expand as their experience grows.
  5. Made security quiet until it matters. MPC-secured social login, biometric and device binding, and a simulation of every transaction before signing.

Results

20M+users, up from 1M
72%wallet activation, up from 45%
$1B+transaction volume
50+chains and 50,000+ tokens supported

What I learned

Good DeFi design keeps powerful controls one deliberate tap away. It never removes them.

Conversion on swaps improved once we stopped designing around chains and started designing around assets and actions.

Trading screens can't simply be shrunk from web to mobile. Information density, touch targets and live data all had to be rethought for the phone.

Leadership, 2014 to now

How I build product and design teams

Most of my career has been as the first senior product or design hire, so building the team and building the product have been the same job. These are the parts of it I can show evidence for.

Designers hired
10+ across four companies
Design systems built
3, at CoinDCX, Fulfil and Pazy
Largest product team
4 designers, 12 engineers, 2 PMs at Okto
Mentees
100+ designers and PMs

Hiring

I've hired 10+ designers across four companies. Each time I set up structured rubrics and an interview loop, so candidates were judged on the same evidence, and paired new hires with a mentor.

At HasGeek I built the design team from scratch. At Pazy a new designer joined an existing system and was shipping within days, which is the test I use for whether onboarding works.

Systems before screens

I've built three design systems. CoinDCX's was adopted by eight product teams and halved design-to-engineering handoff time. Pazy's had 180+ components and 400+ tokens mapped to code before the first production screen, and let engineering grow from 3 to 8 developers while the product stayed consistent.

How decisions get made

At Pazy I ran prioritisation with the founder: every feature scored on pain, frequency and revenue impact, shipped in two-week cycles, and checked against live data in Mixpanel and in Slack channels shared with clients.

At EstateMin I own the roadmap, pricing and revenue target and write the product story for investors. I prototype in code myself, so engineering reviews working software instead of static mockups.

Outside the team

I've given 20+ talks at events, colleges and meetups in India and Ireland, on AI product design, design systems and career growth for senior individual contributors. I've also mentored 100+ PMs and designers.
